∞One Concept, Many Places 28 formula families that repeat across all electrical subjects

Electrical engineering keeps reusing the same few ideas. A transformer, an induction motor and a CT all use the same EMF equation; a synchronous machine and a

transmission line use the same power–angle curve; a transformer and a DC machine reach maximum efficiency by the same rule. Learn each idea once here, then see where it reappears.

How to read each page: ① the core idea in one sentence ② the master formula ③ a table — where it appears, how it is written there, and what to remember ④ a one-line memory hook.

1777:
1Faraday's EMF equation Appears in: Transformer, CT / PT, DC machine, Induction motor, Synchronous machine, Power electronics

Every machine that has a coil and a changing flux makes voltage the same way. Only the name of the machine changes.

e = N·dΦ/dt → for sine flux: E(rms) = 4.44 · f · N · Φm

WhereSame idea written thereRemember
TransformerE₁ = 4.44 f N₁ Φm , E₂ = 4.44 f N₂ Φm → E₁/E₂ = N₁/N₂Φm ∝ V/f. Same V, lower f → core saturates.
Alternator (synchronous gen.)Eph = 4.44 f Φ Tph Kw (Kw = Kp·Kd), f = PN/120Same equation + winding factor (short pitch, distribution).
Induction motorE₁ = 4.44 f N₁ Φ Kw₁ ; rotor running: E₂s = s·E₂ , f₂ = s·fIM = 'rotating transformer' with secondary frequency s·f.
DC machineE = PΦZN / (60A)Same Faraday law; commutator rectifies the AC inside the armature.
CT / PTSame transformer EMF equationCT secondary open → no back mmf → Φ very large → dangerous high voltage.
V/f drivesKeep V/f constant → Φ constantUsed for IM speed control and for testing transformers at lower f.

★ Memory hook: Φ ∝ V/f everywhere — transformer, IM, alternator, V/f drive.

Quick check — exam style

Q. A 230 V, 50 Hz transformer is run at 230 V, 25 Hz. What happens to the core flux?→ Φ ∝ V/f → flux doubles → core saturates, magnetising current becomes very large.
Q. 4-pole, 50 Hz induction motor runs at slip 4 %. Rotor frequency?→ f₂ = s·f = 0.04 × 50 = 2 Hz.
Q. Why must a CT secondary never be opened on load?→ No secondary mmf to cancel primary mmf → flux rises sharply → dangerous high voltage and core overheating.
1778:
2Turns ratio & referring impedance Appears in: Circuits, Transformer, CT / PT, Induction motor, Faults / stability / load flow

When you move a quantity across a turns ratio a = N₁/N₂: voltage × a, current ÷ a, impedance × a².

V₁/V₂ = a , I₁/I₂ = 1/a , Z′ (seen from side 1) = a²·Z₂

WhereSame idea written thereRemember
TransformerR₂′ = a²R₂ , X₂′ = a²X₂ → Req = R₁ + a²R₂Referred circuit = one simple series circuit.
Induction motorR₂′, X₂′ referred to stator exactly like a transformerSame equivalent circuit shape; load resistor R₂′(1−s)/s.
CTI₂ = I₁ × (N₁/N₂) ; burden reflected to primary is tinyCT ratio 400/5 → divide primary current by 80.
PT (VT)V₂ = V₁ × (N₂/N₁)Works almost on no-load (high-impedance meters).
Auto-transformerkVA(auto) = kVA(2-winding) × Vhigh / (Vhigh − Vlow)Only part of the power is transformed → higher rating, higher η.
Per-unit systemZ in ohms changes by (kV ratio)², pu value stays the same on both sidesThat is why pu needs no 'referring'.
Circuits — impedance matchingMax power when a²RL = Rs → a = √(RL/Rs)Same a² rule in audio / RF matching transformers.

★ Memory hook: Voltage × a, current ÷ a, impedance × a².

Quick check — exam style

Q. 10 : 1 transformer, 2 Ω load on the secondary. Impedance seen from the primary?→ a²Z = 10² × 2 = 200 Ω.
Q. CT ratio 400/5 A, primary current 200 A. Secondary current?→ 200 × 5/400 = 2.5 A.
Q. 22 kVA, 2200/220 V transformer reconnected as an auto-transformer for 2420 V. New rating?→ 22 × 2420/220 = 242 kVA.
1779:
3No-load test & short-circuit test Appears in: Transformer, Induction motor, Synchronous machine, DC machine

Every machine is tested the same two ways: (1) no load / open → finds the CONSTANT (iron) loss and magnetising branch; (2) short / blocked → finds the COPPER loss and series impedance.

Open/no-load → P₀ = iron loss, Y₀ ; Short/blocked → Psc = Cu loss, Z =

Vsc / Isc

WhereSame idea written thereRemember
TransformerOC test (on LV side) → core loss, R₀, X₀ ; SC test (on HV side) → full-load Cu loss, Req, ZeqInstruments placed on the side that needs the smallest meters.
Induction motorNo-load test → core + friction loss, Xm ; Blocked-rotor test → R₁+R₂′, X₁+X₂′Blocked rotor = transformer with shorted secondary.
AlternatorOCC + SCC at same field current → Zs = Eoc / IscUnsaturated Zs uses the air-gap line.
DC machineSwinburne's (no-load) test → constant losses ; Hopkinson's test → back-to-backHopkinson (DC) = Sumpner (transformer): two identical machines back-to-back.
Transformer heat runSumpner's (back-to-back) test → temperature rise with only losses drawnSame idea as Hopkinson's test.

★ Memory hook: No-load = iron loss. Short / blocked = copper loss + impedance.

Quick check — exam style

Q. Which transformer test gives the iron (core) loss?→ Open-circuit test.
Q. Blocked-rotor test of an induction motor is like which transformer test?→ Short-circuit test (rotor = shorted secondary).
Q. Hopkinson's test (DC machines) is the same idea as which transformer test?→ Sumpner's back-to-back test.
1780:
4Losses & maximum efficiency Appears in: Transformer, DC machine, Induction motor, Synchronous machine, Transmission line, Measurements

Every machine has a constant loss (iron + friction) and a variable loss (I²R). Efficiency is maximum when the two are EQUAL.

ηmax when Variable loss = Constant loss → load fraction x = √(Pi / Pcu,FL)

WhereSame idea written thereRemember
TransformerCu loss = Iron loss ; x = √(Pi / Pcu,FL) ; Cu loss at x load = x²·Pcu,FLHalf load → Cu loss ÷ 4, iron loss unchanged.
DC machineArmature Cu loss = constant (stray) lossesSame rule.
Induction / synchronousVariable Cu loss = constant core + mechanical lossSame rule.
Transmission (Kelvin's law)Most economical conductor: annual energy-loss cost = annual interest + depreciation on conductor costSame 'variable = fixed' pattern for money.
Iron loss split (all cores)Hysteresis Ph = kh f Bm^1.6 ; Eddy Pe = ke f² Bm² t²At constant V/f: Ph ∝ f, Pe ∝ f². Laminations cut eddy loss.
All-day efficiencykWh output / kWh input over 24 hDistribution transformers: keep iron loss low (always on).

★ Memory hook: Max efficiency when Cu loss = Iron loss — every machine.

Quick check — exam style

Q. Iron loss 1 kW, full-load Cu loss 4 kW. Load for maximum efficiency?→ x = √(1/4) = 0.5 → at 50 % load.
Q. Full-load Cu loss 6400 W. Cu loss at half load?→ 6400 × (½)² = 1600 W (iron loss unchanged).
Q. At constant V/f the frequency is doubled. Hysteresis and eddy losses?→ Hysteresis × 2 (∝ f), eddy × 4 (∝ f²).
1781:
5Voltage regulation — the I(R cosφ + X sinφ) drop Appears in: Transformer, Synchronous machine, Transmission line, DC machine, Cables

Any source with series R and X loses voltage on load by about I(R cosφ ± X sinφ). Lagging load makes it worse; leading load can make it zero or negative.

% Regulation = (Vno-load − Vfull-load) / Vfull-load × 100 ≈ εr cosφ ± εx

sinφ (+ lag, − lead)

WhereSame idea written thereRemember
Transformer%R ≈ εr cosφ + εx sinφ (lag) ; zero when tanφ = εr / εx (leading)εr = % resistance, εx = % reactance.
Alternator%R = (E₀ − V) / V × 100 ; E₀ from V + I·Zs (phasor)Negative regulation at leading pf.
Transmission line%R = (Vs/|A| − Vr) / Vr × 100Light load on long line → negative (Ferranti effect).
DC generator(VNL − VFL) / VFL × 100Shunt: positive; over-compound: can be negative.
Distribution feederDrop = I(R cosφ + X sinφ) per kmSame expression, just per unit length.

★ Memory hook: Lag → big drop. Lead → small/negative drop. Same formula everywhere.

Quick check — exam style

Q. εr = 3 %, εx = 4 %, pf 0.8 lagging. Regulation?→ 3 × 0.8 + 4 × 0.6 = 4.8 %.
Q. Same transformer at 0.8 leading?→ 3 × 0.8 − 4 × 0.6 = 0 % (zero regulation).
Q. Long line on no load: receiving-end voltage higher than sending end. Name?→ Ferranti effect → negative regulation.
1782:
6Power transfer across a reactance (P–δ curve) Appears in: Synchronous machine, Transmission line, Faults / stability / load flow

Real power flows from the LEADING angle to the lagging angle; reactive power flows from HIGHER voltage to lower voltage. Machine or line — same equation.

P = V₁V₂ sinδ / X , Q ≈ V₁(V₁ − V₂ cosδ) / X , Pmax = V₁V₂ / X at δ = 90°

WhereSame idea written thereRemember
Synchronous machine (round rotor)P = E V sinδ / XsGenerator δ > 0 (E leads), motor δ < 0.
Salient-pole machineP = (EV/Xd) sinδ + (V²/2)(1/Xq − 1/Xd) sin2δReluctance part is maximum at δ = 45°.
Transmission line (lossless)P = Vs Vr sinδ / XSteady-state stability limit = Vs Vr / X.
Stability (swing & equal area)(2H/ωs) d²δ/dt² = Pm − Pe ; Aaccelerating = AdeceleratingSame sine curve; fault lowers Pmax.
Load flowP ↔ δ coupling, Q ↔ |V| coupling (fast-decoupled method)Control frequency by P, voltage by Q.
Series compensationXeff = X(1 − k) → Pmax risesSeries capacitor in long lines.

★ Memory hook: P follows angle, Q follows voltage magnitude.

Quick check — exam style

Q. E = V = 1 pu, X = 0.5 pu. Maximum power?→ Pmax = 1 × 1 / 0.5 = 2 pu.
Q. Second identical line added in parallel. Effect on Pmax?→ X halves → Pmax doubles.
Q. 30 % series capacitor compensation. Effect on Pmax?→ Xeff = 0.7 X → Pmax × 1/0.7 ≈ 1.43 times.
1783:
7Reactive power & power factor Appears in: Synchronous machine, Induction motor, Transformer, Transmission line, Faults / stability / load flow

Inductive loads TAKE vars, capacitors GIVE vars. Over-excited synchronous machine behaves like a capacitor; under-excited like an inductor.

Q = V I sinφ ; pf-correction QC = P (tanφ₁ − tanφ₂) ; C = QC / (ωV²)

WhereSame idea written thereRemember
Capacitor bankSupplies QC → raises pf and voltageQC ∝ V² (bank gives less vars at low voltage).
Synchronous motor / condenserOver-excited → leading pf (gives Q) ; V-curve: Ia vs IfMinimum Ia at unity pf (bottom of V-curve).
Induction motor & transformerMagnetising current always lagging → take QLight load → very poor pf.
Induction generatorNeeds Q from grid or capacitorsSelf-excited IG: frequency falls with load.
Transmission lineLine charging (C) gives Q at light load → shunt reactor absorbs itHeavy load → shunt capacitor / series capacitor.
FACTSSVC, STATCOM (shunt Q) ; TCSC, SSSC (series) ; UPFC (both)STATCOM = static synchronous condenser.

★ Memory hook: Over-excited = capacitor. Under-excited = inductor.

Quick check — exam style

Q. 10 kW load, pf 0.6 lag → 0.8 lag. Capacitor kVAr?→ 10 × (tan 53.13° − tan 36.87°) = 10 × (1.333 − 0.75) = 5.83 kVAr.
Q. An over-excited synchronous motor behaves like a …?→ Capacitor — it supplies reactive power (leading pf).
Q. Voltage too high at the end of a lightly loaded long line. Remedy?→ Shunt reactor (absorbs the line-charging vars).
1784:
8Per-unit & short-circuit MVA Appears in: Transformer, Synchronous machine, Faults / stability / load flow, Protection, Transmission line

Per-unit turns every machine and line into the same simple numbers. Fault current is simply 1 / Z(pu).

Zpu = Z(Ω) × MVAbase / kVbase² ; Zpu,new = Zpu,old × (MVAnew/MVAold) ×

(kVold/kVnew)²

WhereSame idea written thereRemember
Transformer% impedance = Zpu × 100 = % short-circuit voltageSame pu on HV and LV sides.
GeneratorXd″ < Xd′ < Xd (sub-transient < transient < steady)First-cycle fault current uses Xd″.
Symmetrical faultIf (pu) = E / Zth ; SC MVA = MVAbase / ZpuN identical generators in parallel → SC MVA × N.
Unsymmetrical faultsLG: If = 3E / (Z₁+Z₂+Z₀+3Zf) ; LL: √3 E / (Z₁+Z₂)Z₀ of generator includes 3Zn.
Circuit breaker ratingBreaking MVA = √3 × kV × kAMaking current = 2.55 × symmetrical breaking current.
Base currentIbase = MVA / (√3 kV)Same formula for every element.

★ Memory hook: Fault MVA = Base MVA / Z(pu).

Quick check — exam style

Q. Z = 0.1 pu on 100 MVA base. Short-circuit MVA?→ 100 / 0.1 = 1000 MVA.
Q. Five 5 MVA alternators, each 25 % reactance, in parallel. SC level at the bus?→ Each 5/0.25 = 20 MVA → 5 × 20 = 100 MVA.
Q. 0.2 pu on 50 MVA. Value on 100 MVA (same kV)?→ 0.2 × 100/50 = 0.4 pu.
1785:
9√(L/C) and 1/√(LC) — one family Appears in: Circuits, Transmission line, Cables, Protection, Power electronics

The same L and C pair gives resonance, surge impedance, wave speed and the critical damping resistor.

f₀ = 1 / (2π√(LC)) , Zc = √(L/C) , v = 1/√(LC) , Rcritical = ½√(L/C)

WhereSame idea written thereRemember
Circuits — resonanceSeries RLC: f₀ = 1/(2π√LC) ; Q = (1/R)√(L/C)At resonance XL = XC, Z = R.
Transmission lineSurge impedance Zc = √(L/C) ≈ 400 Ω (overhead)SIL = V² / Zc.
CableZc ≈ 40–60 Ω (high C)Cable SIL is much higher than overhead line.
Travelling wavesv = 1/√(LC) ≈ 3 × 10⁵ km/s (OHL)Open end → voltage doubles; short → current doubles.
Circuit breakerRestriking frequency f = 1/(2π√LC) ; resistance switching R = ½√(L/C) → no oscillationSame √(L/C) as surge impedance.
Filters / PELC filter corner f = 1/(2π√LC)Same formula.

★ Memory hook: √(L/C) is an impedance; 1/√(LC) is a speed/frequency.

Quick check — exam style

Q. L = 1 mH/km, C = 0.01 μF/km. Surge impedance?→ √(10⁻³ / 10⁻⁸) = √10⁵ ≈ 316 Ω.
Q. 400 kV line, Zc = 400 Ω. SIL?→ V²/Zc = 400² / 400 = 400 MW.
Q. Breaker: L = 50 mH, C = 0.05 μF. Resistor for no restriking oscillation?→ R = ½√(L/C) = ½√(10⁶) = 500 Ω.
1786:
10Time constant & transients Appears in: Circuits, DC machine, Synchronous machine, Faults / stability / load flow, Power electronics, Measurements

Any R–L or R–C path changes exponentially. Time constant decides how fast.

τ = L/R (RL) , τ = RC (RC) ; x(t) = xfinal + (x₀ − xfinal) e^(−t/τ)

WhereSame idea written thereRemember
CircuitsRL / RC charging and dischargingAfter 5τ ≈ steady state (99.3 %).
DC machineField winding τf = Lf / Rf ; armature τa = La / RaLarge field τ → slow build-up of voltage.
Synchronous machine faultsTd″ (few cycles) , Td′ (about 1 s) decaying componentsSub-transient → transient → steady.
Fault DC offsetOffset decays with τ = L/R = X/(ωR) ; maximum when switching at (θ − φ) = ±90°High X/R → slow decay → bigger asymmetry.
Power electronicsInductive load current ripple, snubber RCSame exponential.
MeasurementsInstrument damping, CT saturation with DC offsetSame τ idea.

★ Memory hook: τ = L/R or RC — everywhere something 'rises' or 'decays'.

Quick check — exam style

Q. L = 0.5 H, R = 10 Ω. Time constant and settling time?→ τ = L/R = 50 ms; ≈ 5τ = 0.25 s.
Q. R = 1 MΩ, C = 1 μF. Time constant?→ τ = RC = 1 s.
Q. R = 3.77 Ω, L = 10 mH, v = 150 sin(377t + θ). θ for maximum DC offset?→ X = 3.77 Ω → φ = 45°; max offset at θ = φ − 90° = −45°.
1787:
11Three-phase √3 and 30° Appears in: Circuits, Transformer, Induction motor, Measurements, Protection

Star and delta always bring a √3 and a 30° shift. It appears in transformers, starters, power measurement and protection.

Star: VL = √3 Vph , IL = Iph ; Delta: VL = Vph , IL = √3 Iph ; P = √3 VL IL cosφ

WhereSame idea written thereRemember
Transformer connectionsY-Δ gives 30° phase shift (Dyn11, Yd1 …)Turns ratio is per phase, not per line.
Star-delta starterStarting V ÷ √3 → line current ÷ 3, torque ÷ 3Auto-transformer starter (tap x): current and torque × x².
Impedance conversionZY = Z_Δ / 3Balanced loads only.
Two-wattmeter methodP = W₁ + W₂ ; tanφ = √3 (W₁ − W₂)/(W₁ + W₂)pf < 0.5 → one wattmeter reads negative.
Differential protectionStar-side CTs connected in delta, delta-side CTs in starTo cancel the 30° shift and zero-sequence current.
Third harmonicsCirculate inside delta winding; blocked in star without neutralDelta tertiary winding in Y-Y transformers.

★ Memory hook: Star → line voltage √3; Delta → line current √3; Y-Δ → 30°.

Quick check — exam style

Q. DOL starting current = 6 × full-load. With a star-delta starter?→ 6 / 3 = 2 × full-load (line current).
Q. Two-wattmeter: W₁ = W₂. Power factor? One meter reads zero?→ Equal → pf = 1; one zero → pf = 0.5.
Q. 400 V line, star connection. Phase voltage?→ 400 / √3 ≈ 231 V.
1788:
12Torque, power and V² / I² relations Appears in: Induction motor, Transmission line, Transformer, DC machine, Utilisation

Many 'how does it change' questions are just a square law.

Power ∝ V² (fixed R) ; Loss ∝ I² ; for same power: I ∝ 1/V → line loss ∝

1/V²

WhereSame idea written thereRemember
Induction motor torqueT ∝ s V² R₂ / (R₂² + (sX₂)²) ; Tstart ∝ V² ; Tmax ∝ V² (independent of R₂)s at Tmax = R₂ / X₂ → add rotor R to get Tmax at start.
StartersDOL: I = Isc ; Star-delta: I and T ÷ 3 ; Auto-transformer: × x²Reduced V reduces torque by square.
TransmissionLine loss ∝ 1/V² ; conductor volume ∝ 1/V² (same power, same loss)Why we transmit at high voltage.
Transformer loadingCu loss ∝ (load)² ; iron loss ∝ V² (at fixed f)Half load → Cu loss ÷ 4.
DC motorT ∝ Φ Ia ; N ∝ (V − IaRa)/ΦSeries motor: T ∝ Ia² (unsaturated).
HeatingP = V²/R ; heater at half voltage → ¼ powerSame square law.

★ Memory hook: Halve the voltage → quarter of the power / torque.

Quick check — exam style

Q. Induction motor supply voltage falls by 10 %. Torque?→ T ∝ V² → 0.9² = 0.81 → about 19 % less.
Q. Same power sent at double the voltage. Line loss?→ Loss ∝ 1/V² → ¼ of before.
Q. 1 kW, 230 V heater used at 115 V. Power?→ P ∝ V² → ¼ → 250 W.
1789:
13Synchronous speed, slip & frequency Appears in: Induction motor, Synchronous machine, Utilisation

The rotating field always turns at Ns = 120f/P. Everything else is measured against it.

Ns = 120 f / P , s = (Ns − N)/Ns , rotor frequency f₂ = s·f

WhereSame idea written thereRemember
Induction motor0 < s < 1 ; f₂ = s f ; rotor reactance s X₂s ≈ 2–5 % at full load.
Induction generators < 0 (rotor faster than field)Delivers P, absorbs Q.
Plugging / braking1 < s < 2Reverse field → strong braking.
Synchronous machines = 0 → rotor locked to field ; hunting damped by damper winding (acts like IM cage)Not self-starting; starts as induction motor.
Alternator frequencyf = P N / 1204-pole at 1500 rpm → 50 Hz.
Linear induction motorvs = 2 τ f (τ = pole pitch)Same idea, straight line.
Single-phase IMBackward field slip = 2 − s ; backward rotor frequency (2 − s) fDouble-revolving-field theory.

★ Memory hook: Everything is compared with Ns = 120f/P.

Quick check — exam style

Q. 6-pole, 50 Hz motor at 960 rpm. Slip and rotor frequency?→ Ns = 1000 rpm → s = 4 % → f₂ = 2 Hz.
Q. 8-pole, 50 Hz motor at 727.5 rpm. Rotor emf frequency?→ Ns = 750 → s = 3 % → f₂ = 1.5 Hz.
Q. Linear induction motor, pole pitch 0.5 m, 50 Hz. Synchronous speed?→ v = 2τf = 2 × 0.5 × 50 = 50 m/s = 180 km/h.
1790:
14Balance / difference principle (KCL) Appears in: Protection, Measurements, Circuits

If what goes IN does not equal what comes OUT, something is wrong. Same idea in protection, measurement and earth-leakage devices.

Healthy: Σ Iin = Σ Iout → difference = 0 ; Fault: difference ≠ 0 → operate

WhereSame idea written thereRemember
Differential relay (Merz-Price)Operates on (I₁ − I₂) > bias × averageTransformer, generator, bus bar.
ELCB / RCCBOperates on (Iphase − Ineutral) ≥ 30 mA (people)Same difference idea.
Earth-fault relayResidual current Ia + Ib + Ic = 3I₀Zero in a healthy balanced system.
Wheatstone & AC bridgesBalance: no current in detector → R₁R₄ = R₂R₃Null method → very accurate.
PotentiometerNull deflection → no current drawnSame balance idea.
Translay / pilot-wireCompare currents at both ends of a feederUnit protection.

★ Memory hook: Difference = 0 → healthy. Difference ≠ 0 → trip / unbalance.

Quick check — exam style

Q. Sensitivity of an RCCB used for protection of people?→ 30 mA.
Q. Wheatstone bridge: R₁ = 100 Ω, R₂ = 200 Ω, R₃ = 50 Ω. R₄ at balance (R₁R₄ = R₂R₃)?→ R₄ = 200 × 50 / 100 = 100 Ω.
Q. Healthy balanced 3-phase system: what does a residual earth-fault relay see?→ Ia + Ib + Ic = 0 → no current, no trip.
1791:
15Magnetic circuit — the 'Ohm's law' of flux Appears in: Transformer, CT / PT, DC machine, Induction motor, Synchronous machine, Protection, Circuits

mmf drives flux through reluctance exactly as emf drives current through resistance.

mmf = N I = Φ · S , S = l / (μ₀ μr A) , L = N² / S , M = k √(L₁L₂)

WhereSame idea written thereRemember
TransformerCore with very low S → small magnetising currentAir-core → loose coupling, k < 1.
MachinesAir gap carries most of the reluctanceIM has a small air gap → better pf.
CTCore must not saturate at fault currentKnee-point voltage.
RelaysAttracted-armature: force ∝ I² ; induction disc relaysSame flux idea.
Inductors / chokesAir gap added to avoid saturationSmoothing reactor in PE.
Coupled coilsM = k √(L₁L₂) ; series aiding L₁ + L₂ + 2M , opposing L₁ + L₂ − 2MDot convention.

★ Memory hook: Flux = mmf / reluctance (like I = V/R).

Quick check — exam style

Q. L₁ = 4 mH, L₂ = 9 mH, k = 1. Mutual inductance and series-aiding inductance?→ M = √(4 × 9) = 6 mH; L = 4 + 9 + 2 × 6 = 25 mH.
Q. Turns doubled on the same core. Inductance?→ L ∝ N² → 4 times.
Q. Air gap of a core increased. Effect on magnetising current?→ Reluctance rises → more mmf needed → magnetising current rises.
1792:
16Instruments work like motors Appears in: Measurements, Protection, DC machine, Induction motor

Every deflecting instrument is a small motor that is not allowed to rotate fully. Learn the motor → you know the meter.

Torque T = B I N A (coil in a field) ; T ∝ I² (iron or two coils) ; disc: T ∝

Φ₁Φ₂ sinβ

WhereSame idea written thereRemember
PMMCT = B I N A — exactly the DC motor torqueDC only, uniform scale.
Moving iron (MI)T = ½ I² dL/dθ — reluctance principleAC + DC, square-law scale.
Electrodynamom eterT ∝ I₁ I₂ cosφ dM/dθ — two coils like a motorWattmeter, AC + DC.
Induction energy meterTwo shifted fluxes on a disc — same as induction motor principleBrake magnet = eddy-current damping.
Induction (IDMT) relaySame disc as energy meter; higher current → shorter time (inverse)TMS and PSM settings.
DampingEddy-current damping = same eddy loss as in transformer coresAir friction in MI.

Quick check — exam style

Q. Which instrument reads zero on pure AC?→ PMMC (it responds to the average value).
Q. Deflecting torque of a PMMC instrument?→ T = B I N A — the DC-motor torque.
Q. How is creeping prevented in an induction energy meter?→ Two small holes drilled on opposite sides of the disc.
1793:
17Symmetrical components & earthing Appears in: Transformer, Synchronous machine, Transmission line, Faults / stability / load flow, Protection

Unbalanced currents split into positive, negative and zero sequence. The zero sequence needs a return path (neutral / earth) — delta blocks it.

I₀ = (Ia + Ib + Ic)/3 ; I₁ = (Ia + a Ib + a² Ic)/3 ; I₂ = (Ia + a² Ib + a Ic)/3

WhereSame idea written thereRemember
TransformerZero-sequence path depends on Y-grounded / Δ connectionsΔ: zero-sequence current circulates, no line current.
GeneratorZ₀ includes 3Zn (neutral earthing impedance)Earthing reactor limits LG fault current.
Transmission lineZ₀ ≈ 2–3.5 × Z₁ ; Z₁ = Z₂ (transposed)Static elements: Z₁ = Z₂.
LG faultI₁ = I₂ = I₀ = E / (Z₁+Z₂+Z₀+3Zf)All three in series.
LL faultI₀ = 0 , I₁ = −I₂No earth → no zero sequence.
Negative-sequen ce relayProtects alternator rotor from unbalanced loadingNegative sequence → double-frequency rotor currents.

★ Memory hook: Zero sequence needs an earth path; delta blocks it.

Quick check — exam style

Q. LG fault: E = 1 pu, Z₁ = Z₂ = j0.2, Z₀ = j0.1 pu (solid). Fault current?→ If = 3 × 1 / (0.2 + 0.2 + 0.1) = 6 pu.
Q. Zero-sequence current in the lines on the delta side of a transformer?→ Zero — it only circulates inside the delta.
Q. Ia = Ib = Ic (equal and in phase). Which sequence?→ Only zero sequence.
1794:
18Impedance & reactance Appears in: Circuits, Protection, Synchronous machine, Transformer, Induction motor, Transmission line

R does not change with frequency; XL rises with f; XC falls with f. Many 'what happens if f changes' questions are only this.

Z = R + jX , XL = 2πfL , XC = 1 / (2πfC) , |Z| = √(R² + X²)

WhereSame idea written thereRemember
Distance relayMeasures Z = V / I to the fault (∝ distance)Mho for long, reactance for short lines.
Synchronous machineZs = Ra + jXsXs = Xleakage + Xarmature-reaction.
TransformerZeq = Req + jXeq (referred)X/R ratio decides fault offset.
Induction motorRotor reactance at standstill X₂, running s X₂Low-slip: rotor nearly resistive.
Transmission lineSeries Z = R + jωL per km; shunt Y = jωC per kmABCD from Z and Y.
Harmonicsh-th harmonic: XL × h , XC ÷ hCapacitor banks overload on harmonics.

★ Memory hook: f up → XL up, XC down. R stays the same.

Quick check — exam style

Q. Frequency doubled. XL and XC?→ XL doubles, XC halves.
Q. L = 0.1 H at 50 Hz. Reactance?→ XL = 2π × 50 × 0.1 ≈ 31.4 Ω.
Q. 5th-harmonic voltage on a capacitor bank. Capacitor reactance?→ XC ÷ 5 → it draws 5 times more current per volt.
1795:
19Feedback — one rule for amplifiers, op-amps, oscillators and control Appears in: Circuits, Electronics, Control, Faults / stability / load flow

Feed part of the output back and compare it with the input. Negative feedback trades gain for everything else; positive feedback with loop gain 1 makes an oscillator.

Af = A / (1 + Aβ) · closed loop C/R = G / (1 + GH) · oscillation: Aβ = 1 at

0° (Barkhausen)

WhereSame idea written thereRemember
Transistor amplifierAf = A/(1 + Aβ); bandwidth × (1 + Aβ); distortion and noise ÷ (1 + Aβ)Gain-bandwidth product stays constant.
Feedback topologySeries mixing raises Zin × (1 + Aβ); shunt mixing lowers it; voltage sampling lowers Zout ÷ (1 + Aβ)Voltage-series = the ideal voltage amplifier.
Op-ampHuge A → Af ≈ 1/β: inverting −Rf/R₁, non-inverting 1 + Rf/R₁The resistors, not the op-amp, set the gain.
OscillatorsPositive feedback, |Aβ| = 1, total phase 0° or 360°RC phase-shift needs A ≥ 29; Wien bridge A ≥ 3.
Control systemsC/R = G/(1 + GH); sensitivity to G ÷ (1 + GH); ess falls as loop gain risesSame (1 + loop gain) divider as the amplifier.
Power systemsAVR holds voltage, governor droop shares load (Δf = −R ΔP)Feedback loops on every generator.

★ Memory hook: Negative feedback: gain ÷ (1 + Aβ), bandwidth × (1 + Aβ). Positive feedback with Aβ = 1: oscillator.

Quick check — exam style

Q. A = 100, β = 0.04. Closed-loop gain?→ Af = 100/(1 + 4) = 20.
Q. Loop gain Aβ = 1 at 0° phase. Result?→ Sustained oscillation (Barkhausen criterion).
Q. Unity feedback, G = 10. C/R?→ 10/11 ≈ 0.909.
1796:
20RMS, average, form factor & peak factor Appears in: Circuits, Measurements, Power electronics, Electronics

RMS is the heating value, average is what a moving-coil meter sees. Their ratio (form factor) tells you which waveform you have.

Vrms = √(mean of v²) , Vavg = mean of |v| , form factor = Vrms / Vavg ,

peak factor = Vm / Vrms

WhereSame idea written thereRemember
SineVrms = Vm/√2 = 0.707 Vm; Vavg = 2Vm/π = 0.637 Vm; FF 1.11, PF 1.414The numbers on every AC nameplate are rms.
Square waveVrms = Vavg = Vm; FF 1, PF 1Flat top → rms = peak.
Triangle / sawtoothVrms = Vm/√3; Vavg = Vm/2; FF 1.155, PF 1.732√3 for a straight-line ramp.
RectifiersHalf-wave: Vdc = Vm/π, Vrms = Vm/2 (FF 1.57). Full-wave: Vdc = 2Vm/π, Vrms = Vm/√2Ripple factor = √(FF² − 1): 1.21 half-wave, 0.48 full-wave.
MeasurementsMoving iron and dynamometer read rms; PMMC reads average; rectifier meters are scaled by 1.11A non-sine wave on a rectifier meter → error.
Power electronicsChopper output: Vavg = D·V, Vrms = √D·VAverage sets dc power; rms sets heating.
DC + harmonicsVrms = √(V₀² + V₁² + V₂² + …) (each in rms)Add squares, never the values.

★ Memory hook: Heating → rms; meter needle (PMMC) → average; sine FF = 1.11.

Quick check — exam style

Q. Half-wave rectified sine, peak 100 V. Average and rms?→ Vavg = 100/π = 31.83 V; Vrms = 50 V.
Q. Square wave of ±10 V on an average-responding meter scaled for sine. Reading?→ Average 10 V × 1.11 = 11.1 V (true rms is 10 V).
Q. v = 10 + 10√2 sin ωt. RMS value?→ √(10² + 10²) = 14.14 V.
1797:
21Duty ratio & averaging Appears in: Power electronics, Electronics, Measurements, Utilisation

Switch a voltage on for a fraction D of each period and the load sees the average. Every chopper, PWM drive and 555 timer works this way.

Average = D·Vhigh + (1 − D)·Vlow , rms of a pulse train = V√D

WhereSame idea written thereRemember
Buck chopperV₀ = D·VsD = 0.4 on 100 V → 40 V.
Boost · buck-boostV₀ = Vs/(1 − D) · V₀ = D·Vs/(1 − D) (inverted)D → 1 makes the boost output shoot up.
PWM inverterFundamental ∝ modulation index m (linear for m ≤ 1)Average over each carrier period follows the sine.
555 astablef = 1.44/((RA + 2RB)C); D = (RA + RB)/(RA + 2RB)D is always above 50 % unless a diode bypasses RB.
Integral-cycle controlP = Pfull · n/(n + m); Vrms = V√(n/(n + m))Same √D rule for the rms.
Pulse train · digital clockVavg = D·V; fundamental and harmonics set by DD = 50 % kills the even harmonics.

★ Memory hook: Average = D × V; rms = √D × V.

Quick check — exam style

Q. Buck chopper, Vs = 100 V, D = 0.4. Output?→ 40 V.
Q. Pulse train 10 V, D = 0.25. Average and rms?→ Average 2.5 V; rms 10√0.25 = 5 V.
Q. 555 astable, RA = 1 kΩ, RB = 2 kΩ, C = 0.1 µF. f and D?→ f = 1.44/(5 kΩ × 0.1 µF) ≈ 2880 Hz; D = 3/5 = 60 %.

22Decibels — one ratio scale everywhere Appears in: Electronics, Control, Communication, Measurements, Transmission line

dB turns multiplication into addition. Use 10 log for power ratios and 20 log for voltage or current ratios.

dB = 10 log₁₀(P₂/P₁) = 20 log₁₀(V₂/V₁) ; dBm = 10 log₁₀(P / 1 mW) ; 1

neper = 8.686 dB

WhereSame idea written thereRemember
AmplifiersStage gains in dB simply add20 dB + 30 dB = 50 dB (voltage × 316).
Bode plotsEach pole −20 dB/decade (−6 dB/octave); corner is the −3 dB point−3 dB = half power, 0.707 of the voltage.

PCMSQNR ≈ 6.02n + 1.76 dBEach extra bit adds 6 dB.
Op-ampsCMRR (dB) = 20 log(Ad/Ac)A CMRR of 100 dB = a ratio of 10⁵.

Quick check — exam style

Q. Stages of 20 dB and 30 dB in cascade. Overall voltage gain?→ 50 dB = ×316.
Q. 1 W in dBm?→ 30 dBm.
Q. Power halves. Change in dB?→ −3.01 dB.

23Thevenin view — any network is a source behind an impedance Appears in: Circuits, Faults / stability / load flow, Induction motor, Synchronous machine, Electronics, Measurements

Seen from two terminals, a linear network is one voltage behind one impedance. Engineers use this picture in circuits, faults, machines and electronics alike.

Vth = open-circuit voltage , Zth = Voc / Isc (or the impedance with

sources killed)

WhereSame idea written thereRemember
CircuitsMaximum power when RL = Rth: Pmax = Vth²/(4Rth)Norton: IN = Vth/Rth, same R.
Fault calculationFault current = Vprefault / Zth; Z-bus diagonal element = Zth at that busShort-circuit MVA = base MVA / Zth (pu).
Induction motorStator side replaced by Vth, Zth → smax = R₂′/√(Rth² + (Xth + X₂′)²)Exact torque formula uses the Thevenin stator.
Alternator & gridE behind Xs; the grid is an infinite bus (Zth → 0)Stiff bus = tiny Thevenin impedance.
Transistor biasDivider: Vth = Vcc R₂/(R₁ + R₂), Rth = R₁ ∥ R₂Then IB = (Vth − VBE)/(Rth + (β + 1)RE).
MeasurementsVoltmeter loading: reading = Vth · Rv/(Rv + Rth)High-R source + low-R meter → low reading.

★ Memory hook: Open-circuit voltage + short-circuit current = the whole network.

Quick check — exam style

Q. Voc = 12 V, Isc = 3 A. Load for maximum power and Pmax?→ Rth = 4 Ω → RL = 4 Ω, Pmax = 12²/(4 × 4) = 9 W.
Q. Pre-fault 1 pu, Zth = j0.25 pu. Three-phase fault current?→ 1/0.25 = 4 pu.
Q. Divider R₁ = 40 kΩ, R₂ = 10 kΩ on 10 V. Vth and Rth?→ Vth = 2 V; Rth = 40 ∥ 10 = 8 kΩ.
1800:
24Harmonics — one Fourier idea in power, machines and electronics Appears in: Power electronics, Faults / stability / load flow, Transformer, Synchronous machine, Circuits, Measurements

Any periodic non-sine wave is a fundamental plus harmonics. Odd symmetry keeps only odd harmonics; three-phase circuits trap or add the triplens.

THD = √(V₂² + V₃² + …) / V₁ , Vrms = V₁√(1 + THD²) , pf = (I₁/Irms)·cos φ₁

WhereSame idea written thereRemember
Square waveOnly odd harmonics, amplitude 4V/(nπ)Fourier series of half-wave symmetry.
Converters6-pulse: 6k ± 1 (5, 7, 11, 13 …); 12-pulse: 12k ± 1 (11, 13 …)More pulses → cleaner current.
TransformersMagnetising current carries a 3rd harmonic; a delta winding traps triplensStar-star needs a delta tertiary.
Three-phase 4-wireTriplens are in phase in all lines → IN = 3I₃Neutral can carry more than a line.
AC machinesShort pitch by 1/n of a pole pitch removes the nth harmonic (kp = cos(nα/2))Distribution factor cuts them further.
Capacitors & filtersXC ÷ n at the nth harmonic → large harmonic current, resonance riskDetuned (series L) capacitor banks.
MeasurementsAverage-reading meters err on harmonics; use true-rms metersForm factor no longer 1.11.

★ Memory hook: Odd symmetry → odd harmonics; triplens add in the neutral, vanish in delta.

Quick check — exam style

Q. V₁ = 100, V₃ = 30, V₅ = 40 (rms). THD?→ √(30² + 40²)/100 = 50 %.
Q. Line-current harmonics of a 6-pulse converter?→ 6k ± 1: 5, 7, 11, 13 …
Q. Coil pitch that removes the 5th harmonic?→ Short pitch by 1/5 of a pole pitch (kp5 = cos 90° = 0).
1801:
25Sampling & aliasing Appears in: Signals & DSP, Communication, Measurements, Electronics

Sample at least twice the highest frequency, or a high tone shows up disguised as a low one.

fs ≥ 2 fmax (Nyquist) , a tone at f appears at |f − k·fs| , PCM bit rate = n ·

fs

WhereSame idea written thereRemember
DSPAnti-alias low-pass filter before the ADC; reconstruction by ideal low-passSpectrum repeats every fs.
PCMfs ≥ 2W; bit rate n·fs; bandwidth ≥ n·fs/2Voice: 8 kHz × 8 bits = 64 kb/s.
Product of signalsBandwidth of x₁·x₂ = B₁ + B₂ → Nyquist rate 2(B₁ + B₂)Squaring doubles the bandwidth.
Band-pass samplingfs ≥ 2B (bandwidth), not 2fmax, under the band-position conditionUsed for radio IF signals.
Digital instrumentsSample-and-hold, then ADC; conversion must finish in 1/fsSampling scopes rebuild fast repetitive waves.
StroboscopeA rotating disc lit at fs looks still when its rate = k·fsAliasing used on purpose to measure speed.

★ Memory hook: Twice the top frequency; alias = |f − k fs|.

Quick check — exam style

Q. cos(2π·300t) sampled at 400 Hz. Apparent frequency?→ |300 − 400| = 100 Hz.
Q. 4 kHz voice, 8 bits per sample, Nyquist sampling. Bit rate?→ 8 kHz × 8 = 64 kb/s.
Q. Signals of 1 kHz and 3 kHz bandwidth are multiplied. Nyquist rate?→ 2 × (1 + 3) = 8 kHz.

26Coupling coefficient, mutual inductance & leakage Appears in: Circuits, Transformer, Induction motor, Measurements, Communication, Transmission line

Two coils share part of their flux. The shared part is mutual inductance; the part that misses is leakage. k tells how much is shared.

M = k√(L₁L₂) , aiding L = L₁ + L₂ + 2M , opposing L = L₁ + L₂ − 2M , W =

½L₁I₁² + ½L₂I₂² ± M I₁I₂

WhereSame idea written thereRemember
Coupled coilsM = (Laiding − Lopposing)/4; dot convention sets the signk ≤ 1 always.
Transformerk ≈ 1 → small leakage reactance; ideal transformer k = 1Leakage gives the series reactance X₁ + X₂′.
Induction motorAir gap → larger magnetising current and more leakage than a transformerLeakage reactance limits Tmax.
MeasurementsMutual inductors, Campbell bridge, Rogowski coilM measured by aiding/opposing method.
CommunicationTuned IF transformers are loosely coupled (k < 1) to shape bandwidthCritical coupling k = 1/Q.
Transmission linesMutual coupling between parallel circuits; zero-sequence mutual is largeAffects earth-fault relay reach.

★ Memory hook: Shared flux = M; missed flux = leakage; M = k√(L₁L₂).

Quick check — exam style

Q. L₁ = 4 mH, L₂ = 9 mH, M = 3 mH. Coupling coefficient?→ k = 3/√36 = 0.5.
Q. Series aiding 30 mH, opposing 14 mH. M?→ (30 − 14)/4 = 4 mH.
Q. Why does an induction motor draw a larger magnetising current than a transformer?→ The air gap raises the reluctance.

27Q factor & bandwidth Appears in: Circuits, Electronics, Communication, Measurements, Control

Q compares the energy a resonant circuit stores with the energy it loses each cycle. High Q means a sharp peak and a narrow band.

Q = 2π × (energy stored)/(energy lost per cycle) ; series: Q = ω₀L/R =

1/(ω₀CR) ; BW = f₀/Q

WhereSame idea written thereRemember
Series RLCVoltage magnification: VC = VL = Q·V at resonanceQ = (1/R)√(L/C).
Parallel RLCCurrent magnification: IC = IL = Q·IQ = R√(C/L).
CoilsQ = ωL/R measured with a Q meterLosses lower Q.
Tuned amplifiersBW = f₀/Q; cascading identical stages narrows the bandSelectivity of radio IF stages.
Second-order systemsζ = 1/(2Q); resonant peak Mr = 1/(2ζ√(1 − ζ²))Low damping = high Q = big peak.
FiltersQ = f₀/(f₂ − f₁) between the −3 dB pointsSame formula for band-pass filters.

★ Memory hook: Q = f₀/BW = 1/(2ζ).

Quick check — exam style

Q. Series R = 10 Ω, L = 0.1 H, C = 10 µF. f₀, Q, bandwidth?→ ω₀ = 1000 rad/s (f₀ ≈ 159.2 Hz), Q = 10, BW ≈ 15.9 Hz.
Q. Second-order system with ζ = 0.25. Q?→ Q = 1/(2ζ) = 2.
Q. Series resonance, Q = 50, source 10 V. Capacitor voltage?→ Q × V = 500 V.

28Stored energy — ½ × stiffness × (quantity)² Appears in: Circuits, Faults / stability / load flow, Synchronous machine, Utilisation, DC machine

Capacitors, inductors and rotating masses all store energy with the same ½·k·x² form.

W = ½CV² = Q²/2C (electric) , W = ½LI² (magnetic) , W = ½Jω²

(rotating) , energy density ½εE², B²/2μ

WhereSame idea written thereRemember
Capacitor½CV²; charge sharing between capacitors always loses energyTwo equal C, one charged: half the energy is lost.
Inductor½LI²; breaking the current releases it as a spark / voltage spikeFreewheeling diode gives it a safe path.
FieldsElectric ½εE² per m³, magnetic B²/(2μ) per m³Force on a magnet ∝ B²·A/(2μ₀).

MechanicsSpring ½kx²; flywheel ½Jω²Same squared form.

Q. 100 µF charged to 200 V. Energy?→ ½ × 100 µF × 200² = 2 J.
Q. 0.5 H coil carrying 4 A. Energy?→ ½ × 0.5 × 4² = 4 J.
Q. 10 µF at 100 V joined to an equal uncharged 10 µF. Energy before and after?→ 0.05 J → 0.025 J (half is lost in the connection).
